title: Breakthrough HIV Prevention Drug Could Slash Infections, but Funding Cuts Block Access
excerpt: Lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injection with near-perfect efficacy, is reaching only a fraction of those who need it as USAID and global donor pullbacks cripple distribution.
body:
• Lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injectable, has shown near 100 percent effectiveness in preventing HIV infection in clinical trials, offering a transformative alternative to daily oral PrEP.
  • The Global Fund and the US have expanded their commitment to reach 3 million people with lenacapavir by 2028, but early rollout has reached only nine African countries so far.
  • Gilead sells lenacapavir at $28,000 per year in the US, though studies show generic versions could be produced for as little as $25 per person per year.
  • Doctors Without Borders says Gilead has refused to sell the drug directly to humanitarian organizations, directing them instead to limited Global Fund supplies.

A Medical Breakthrough Bottlenecked

The science is unambiguous: lenacapavir, a long-acting injectable capsid inhibitor made by Gilead Sciences, demonstrated near-total effectiveness in preventing HIV infection across multiple clinical trials. Given just twice a year as a subcutaneous injection, it overcomes the adherence challenges that have plagued daily oral PrEP pills for years.

But the drug's real-world impact is being strangled by a collision of corporate pricing decisions, donor funding cuts, and distribution barriers that are keeping it out of reach for the vast majority of people who need it.

The Access Gap

The Global Fund and the United States expanded their commitment in April to reach 3 million people with lenacapavir by 2028. Initial deliveries have reached nine African countries, with plans to extend to 12 more. Early data shows strong uptake among priority populations, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescent girls, and first-time PrEP users.

But the scale of the response remains tiny relative to the need. Researchers estimate that 54 to 55 million people per year could benefit from lenacapavir globally. The 3 million target addresses less than 6 percent of potential demand.

"Any expanded access to lenacapavir is a good thing, but reaching only one million more people in three years is a tiny fraction of what's needed to make a real dent in the HIV epidemic."

— Dr. Tom Ellman, Director, MSF Southern Africa Medical Unit

Price and Politics

Gilead charges $28,000 per year per patient in the United States for lenacapavir. Research published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases shows generic versions could be manufactured for $25 per person per year at scale. Gilead has granted voluntary licenses to several manufacturers for low-income countries, but a quarter of new HIV infections occur in countries excluded from these agreements.

Doctors Without Borders has been trying for a year to purchase lenacapavir directly from Gilead, but the company has repeatedly refused, directing MSF to the Global Fund's limited supply — which has already run short in countries like Eswatini and Kenya.
nri_angle: Indian American physicians and global health researchers are at the forefront of lenacapavir advocacy, while Indian generic manufacturers hold the key to making the drug affordable worldwide.
author: Diaspora Desk
